headline: Flash-panning: romance that starts hot, ends in silence

sources.title: Flashpanning Is Yet Another Troubling Dating Trend Fueled By Commitment-Phobes (Glam)
Dating Games: 5 Signs of a 'Flashpanner' (video, Susan Winter)

chunks.text: Dating experts have a name for a [[romance]] that starts fast and ends in silence: [[flash-panning]]. The [[pattern]] begins like a movie. Two people meet and {{hit it off}} so well that they talk every night and see each other every day. There are gifts, dates, and big [[promises]]. One person is [[swept off their feet]] and {{falls for}} the other completely. The new [[couple]] even {{show off}} the romance online, where every photo looks like a [[perfect match]]. Then, within weeks, one partner vanishes, and the ending is [[cruel]].

verbs.correct: To like each other right away
verbs.wrong: To meet someone for the first time
verbs.why: Two strangers can hit it off at a party, and new coworkers sometimes hit it off on the very first day. This couple hit it off so well that they were talking every night and seeing each other daily.

A neighbor can fall for the person who walks her dog every morning, and sometimes people fall for someone before they really know that person. One person falls for the other quickly, charmed by gifts, dates, and big promises before ordinary life begins.

verbs.wrong: To arrive at a planned meeting
verbs.why: Kids show off a new bike to friends, and travelers show off vacation photos online. This couple showed off their romance online, where every picture looked like a perfect match.

chunks.text: Then [[ordinary]] life {{comes along}}: work schedules, tired evenings, and small [[disagreements]]. For most couples, this is where the real work of love begins. For a flashpanner, it is the [[exit]]. The excitement {{wears off}}, and the flashpanner begins {{pulling away}}, answering less and less each day. Soon that partner disappears completely, without a fight and without an [[explanation]]. The person {{left behind}} keeps asking the same question: what did I do wrong?

verbs.why: A good opportunity can come along when you least expect it, and sometimes trouble comes along just as things feel settled. Here ordinary life comes along, with work schedules, tired evenings, and small disagreements.

verbs.wrong: To make someone tired over time
verbs.why: The excitement of a new job can wear off after a few months, and the thrill of new shoes can wear off after one wear. For a flashpanner, the early excitement wears off the moment real life starts.

A friend can pull away after moving to a new city, and a quiet student may pull away from the rest of the class over a long semester. The flashpanner starts pulling away by answering messages later and later each day.

verbs.correct: To go and not take someone with you
verbs.wrong: To carry someone a long way
verbs.why: A fast hiker can leave behind slower friends on a trail, and a school bus can leave behind a student who arrives one minute late. A flashpanner disappears completely and leaves the other person behind, confused and hurt.

chunks.text: Why do people do this? Relationship expert Susan Winter says flashpanners love the [[electric]] first weeks but cannot {{deal with}} boring Tuesdays and real [[compromise]]. Many never learned that small fights are a normal part of love, and the root cause is a fear of commitment. They will not {{open up}} about a problem; they simply vanish. The pattern is not new: a radio station website described it in 2019, and Winter explained it in 2023. It starts like [[love bombing]], with [[extreme]] attention and gifts, but the flashpanner leaves within weeks, and the romance usually ends in [[ghosting]].

verbs.why: Nurses deal with stress every shift, and parents deal with tantrums calmly. Flashpanners love the exciting first weeks but cannot deal with boring Tuesdays and the compromise real love needs.

verbs.wrong: To make a joke of something
verbs.why: Close friends open up about their fears late at night, and therapy helps some people open up for the first time. Flashpanners will not open up about a problem; instead of talking, they simply vanish.

chunks.text: The harm is real. After weeks of [[closeness]], the sudden silence is deeply painful. It is hard to {{get over}} someone who simply disappeared, and many people are left with less trust in dating. Experts say the best [[defense]] is to be honest about what you want and to take things slowly, with a little [[patience]]. So {{watch out for}} the [[warning signs]]: a [[flawless]] first week, gifts and big promises, and [[excitement]] that feels too strong too soon. Real love grows more slowly, and it survives boring Tuesdays.

verbs.correct: To feel better after something bad
verbs.wrong: To stop talking to someone on purpose
verbs.why: It takes time to get over a bad cold, and some people never fully get over their first heartbreak. It is hard to get over someone who disappeared without any explanation.

verbs.correct: To be careful about a danger
verbs.why: Drivers watch out for ice on the road, and shoppers watch out for hidden fees on cheap deals. Experts say to watch out for a flawless first week, early gifts, and promises that feel too big too soon.

mainIdea.s: Flash-panning is a dating pattern where someone starts a romance with great energy and then disappears when ordinary life begins. Experts say daters should learn the signs.
mainIdea.why: Flash-panning starts with an intense few weeks and ends in a sudden exit when work schedules and small disagreements arrive.

mainIdea.s: In flash-panning, a romance begins with intense attention and ends in sudden silence. Experts blame the other partner, who pushes for a serious commitment far too soon.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the cause is the flashpanner's own fear of commitment, not pressure from the partner. Flashpanners cannot deal with boring days and real compromise.

mainIdea.s: A dating app added a tool that warns users when a new match sends too many messages too quickly. Millions of daters have already turned the new warning on their phones.
mainIdea.why: No dating app or new tool is involved. Flash-panning is a dating pattern, and the advice is to watch out for its warning signs.

tf.s: In a flash-panning romance, the first days are quiet and slow.
tf.why: The start is intense. The two people hit it off fast, with constant dates, texts, and big promises.

tf.s: Flashpanners often pull away when everyday problems come along.
tf.why: When schedules and small disagreements appear, the excitement wears off and they start to disappear.

tf.s: The expert says many flashpanners never learned that small fights are normal in love.
tf.why: She says they cannot deal with the boring days and compromise that real relationships need.

tf.s: The flashpanner usually leaves after several months.
tf.why: The flashpanner pulls away within weeks, and the romance usually ends in ghosting.

tf.s: The advice is to watch out for a romance that feels perfect from day one.
tf.why: A flawless first week, early gifts, and big promises can be warning signs.

lines.text: Have you heard of flash-panning? Dating experts have a name for a romance that starts like a movie and ends in silence.
Two people {{hit it off}}, talk every night, see each other every day. Gifts, dates, big promises. One of them {{falls for}} the other completely.
And they {{show off}} the whole thing online, I bet. Perfect photos, perfect couple.
Every time. Then ordinary life {{comes along}}: work schedules, tired evenings, small disagreements. For a flashpanner, that's the exit.
So the whole romance is [[a flash in the pan]]. Hot for a minute, then nothing.
Exactly. The excitement {{wears off}}, they start {{pulling away}}, and within weeks they're gone. No fight, no explanation.
My cousin had that happen to him. He got a gift almost every day for weeks, and then she vanished [[out of the blue]].
Being {{left behind}} like that is the part that really hurts. You keep asking what you did wrong.
He asked it for months. It took him a long time to {{get over}} her, and he still doesn't trust dating much.

The article says that's the real harm. And the answer is usually nothing. Susan Winter, a relationship expert, says flashpanners love the electric first weeks but can't {{deal with}} boring Tuesdays and compromise.
So [[it's all for show]]. Why not just say something instead of disappearing?

Winter says the cause is a fear of commitment. Many of them never learned that small fights are a normal part of love, so they won't {{open up}} about a problem. It starts like love bombing, all that extreme attention and gifts, and it usually ends in ghosting.
So it's ghosting with a fancier name. Is this even new?

Not at all. A radio station website described it in 2019, and Winter explained it in 2023. The advice is the same, too: be honest about what you want, take things slowly, and {{watch out for}} a flawless first week and excitement that feels too strong too soon.
[[Old news]], then, and [[slow and steady wins the race]]. If someone still wants to see you on a boring Tuesday, that's the real thing.

expressions.def: Something that is exciting or successful for a very short time and then disappears
ex: The band had one hit song and then vanished. A flash in the pan.
Everyone thought the new cafe was a flash in the pan, but it's still busy.
She called me out of the blue after ten years.
The company closed the office out of the blue.

expressions.def: Used to say that something is done only to impress people and is not sincere
ex: His big gifts were nice, but it's all for show.
The new office looks great, but it's all for show.

expressions.def: Information that people already know, so it is not surprising or interesting anymore
ex: The merger? That's old news, it was announced weeks ago.
Everyone at school already knows about the party. It's old news.

expressions.expr: slow and steady wins the race
expressions.def: Used to say that careful, patient effort works better than rushing
ex: I only study an hour a day, but slow and steady wins the race.
He didn't sprint at the start of the marathon. Slow and steady wins the race.
